Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run in a CI job) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that you’ll need to add to the repo.

> **⚠️** I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git add`, `git commit` or `git push` from here – you’ll have to execute those commands on your machine or in your CI environment.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick scan to see what the repo contains:

```bash
# List top‑level files
ls -al

# Show the main entry point (usually index.js or app.js)
cat package.json | grep -E '"main"|"start"'
```

> For a typical “nodejs‑welcome” repo you’ll probably see:
> * `package.json`
> * `app.js` (or `index.js`)
> * `README.md`
> * maybe a `src/` folder

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json (if present)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install app dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and stable.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> * Exposes port **3000** – the default for many Node apps.  
> * Uses `npm start` which should match the script defined in `package.json`.

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAML files

Create a directory called `k8s` (or `deployments`) and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use another registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app inside the cluster on port 80 (forwarded to container port 3000).  
> * Uses `ClusterIP` – change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Docker Buildx
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the Docker image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

      # Optional: Deploy to a Kubernetes cluster (e.g., via kubectl)
      # Uncomment and configure the following if you want automatic deployment
      #
      # - name: Set up kubectl
      #   uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
      #   with:
      #     version: 'latest'
      #
      # - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      #   env:
      #     KUBECONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
      #   run: |
      #     kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

> **Key points**  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> * Builds the image from the repo root (`context: .`).  
> * Tags the image as `ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>:latest`.  
> * Pushes the image automatically on every push to `main`.  
> * The optional deployment section is commented out – enable it if you have a K8s cluster and a `KUBECONFIG` secret.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
# Stage the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Verify the staged files
git status
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repo
git push origin main
```

> If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Exposes the app inside the cluster |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Automates Docker build & push on pushes to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the image tag, registry, or deployment details to match your environment. Happy coding!
